title: Short Stuff: Edward Mordake
summary: Short Stuff episode on Edward Mordake, the supposed 19th-century man with a shrunken second face on the back of his head. The hosts explain the story originated as a fabricated 1895 Boston Sunday Post article by Charles Lowton Hildreth, which was later copied as fact into an 1896 medical book by two doctors. They cover the real rare conditions of craniofacial duplication (diprosopus) and craniopagus parasiticus, including cases in India (2008) and Egypt (Manar Maged), the fake mummified-head gaff by Edwin Weret Schindler, the Tom Waits song and American Horror Story portrayal, and how the hoax spread on Facebook.

entities.name: The Anomalies and Curiosities of Medicine

segments.title: Opening banter and name pronunciation
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the Jerry mascot on the back of their heads, then clarify that the name is spelled and pronounced Mordake, not Moredrake.

segments.title: The 1895 Boston Sunday Post article
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1895 Boston Sunday Post article by Charles Lowton Hildreth, headlined The Wonders of Modern Science, which claimed a Royal Scientific Society had reported on half-human monsters, including a half-crab man and the Norfolk spider with a human head.

segments.title: The article was fiction
segments.summary: The hosts explain the article was made up. Hildreth was a science writer and poet, and the paper is compared to the National Inquirer or Weekly World News. Hildreth died a year later, in 1896.

segments.title: Copied into a medical book as fact
segments.summary: In 1896 two doctors published The Anomalies and Curiosities of Medicine, claiming exhaustive research, and copied Hildreth's Mordake entry word for word as fact. The hosts recount the story: a handsome scholar tormented by an evil twin face whose lips moved and eyes followed people, who asked doctors to crush it and then poisoned himself at 23, leaving a note.

segments.title: The devil twin and real craniofacial conditions
segments.summary: Chuck notes the devil twin was described as a girl. He explains that such conditions are real but extremely rare: craniofacial duplication (diprosopus), with fewer than fifty known cases since 1864, most stillborn, and it also occurs in animals.

segments.title: Real cases: India 2008 and Manar Maged
segments.summary: Josh describes a baby girl born in India in 2008 with two faces who was worshiped as a reincarnation of Durga and reportedly died at two months. He also describes Manar Maged of Egypt, born in 2005, who had craniopagus parasiticus, in which a parasitic twin attached to the back of the head drains the host; at least three such cases have had the twin removed.

segments.title: Pop culture and the fake mummified head
segments.summary: Chuck describes the rarity of craniopagus parasiticus, about six in ten million births. He mentions a Tom Waits song called Poor Edward and a character in American Horror Story: Freak Show. He identifies the widely shared mummified head photo as a gaff made by Edwin Weret Schindler.

segments.title: How the hoax spread online
segments.summary: Josh says the story and photos were shared on Facebook as real, at least 260,000 times, and people did not question whether it was true. He calls this a current problem of believing unverified claims.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes the episode with the show credits.
